The annual Manimahesh Yatra, coinciding with Janmashtami (August-September), is one of the most important pilgrimages in North India. The lake remains frozen for most of the year and is surrounded by perpetual snow. The Chamba royals were the traditional patrons of this pilgrimage, and the town of Chamba hosts elaborate processions before the Yatra begins.

Kartik Swami's temple follows traditional Himachali pagoda architecture with multi-tiered slate roofs and intricate wooden carvings depicting mythological scenes. The deity's jurisdiction covers surrounding hamlets where the oracle (Gur) communicates divine will through trance-based possession rituals. During the world-famous Kullu Dussehra, Kartik Swami's ornate palanquin (Rath) joins the grand procession to pay homage to Lord Raghunath Ji at Dhalpur Maidan. The deity's silver mohra (face mask) and ceremonial ornaments are treasured hereditary possessions maintained by the temple committee (Devta Kardar). Housed in the high-altitude Kanawar sanctuary; son of Lord Shiva. Local worship involves elaborate seasonal rituals marking the agricultural calendar, with special ceremonies during planting and harvest seasons.
column11: To reach the temple in Kanawar, you can take a bus or taxi from the main Kullu bus stand. The nearest airport is Bhuntar Airport (Kullu-Manali), and the closest major railhead is Jogindernagar Railway Station / Chandigarh. Local transport (HRTC buses and private cabs) connect the district headquarters to the village.

column5: Shringa Rishi is the presiding deity of the Banjar Valley in Kullu, identified with the sage Rishyashringa from the Ramayana. According to the epic, King Dasharatha invited Rishyashringa to perform the Putrakameshti Yagna (fire sacrifice) that resulted in the birth of Lord Rama and his brothers. This makes Shringa Rishi directly responsible for one of the most pivotal events in Hindu mythology. His temple in Banjar features exquisite wood carvings and a silver palanquin adorned with multiple gold-plated mohras (face masks). The deity's annual rath yatra through the Banjar valley is one of the most colorful events in the region, with dozens of village deities joining the procession. Shringa Rishi's oracle is known for accurate predictions about rainfall and harvests.

column5: Manu Rishi Temple in Manali is the only temple in India dedicated to Sage Manu, the progenitor of humanity according to Hindu mythology. The name 'Manali' itself derives from 'Manu-Alaya' (Abode of Manu). According to legend, Sage Manu stepped off his ark at this very spot after the great deluge that destroyed the world, making Manali the cradle of human civilization. The temple sits on a hilltop in Old Manali, surrounded by ancient Deodar cedar forests. The stone and wood structure features traditional Himachali architecture with a multi-tiered slate roof. Inside, the sage is depicted seated in deep meditation. The temple is significant not only religiously but also historically, as it establishes the mythological importance of the Kullu Valley as the place where human civilization was reborn after the apocalyptic flood described in the Matsya Purana.

column5: Adi Brahma of Khokhan is one of the most ancient deities in the Kullu Valley, housed in a massive four-tiered pagoda-style temple that is an architectural wonder of Himalayan craftsmanship. The temple features elaborate wood carvings depicting scenes from Hindu mythology, geometric patterns, and celestial beings. Adi Brahma is considered a primordial creator deity, and the Khokhan temple is one of the rare temples in India dedicated to Brahma. The deity's jurisdiction extends over several villages in the Parvati Valley region. During festivals, the deity is carried in a beautifully decorated palanquin (Rath) with silver ornaments. The temple's stone foundation dates back several centuries, with the wooden superstructure rebuilt periodically. Local tradition holds that the deity chose this location after wandering across the Himalayan valleys seeking the perfect seat of power.

column5: Jamlu Devta (also Jamdagni Rishi) is the fiercely independent deity of the ancient village of Malana, often called the oldest democracy in the world. Unlike all other deities in the Kullu Valley, Jamlu does not pay homage to Lord Raghunath Ji during Dussehra, asserting his sovereign independence. The Malana village operates under its own parliament (the 'Malana Niti') with Jamlu as the supreme authority. All disputes are settled by the deity's oracle, and outsiders are forbidden from touching temple property. The villagers believe they are descendants of Alexander the Great's soldiers, and Jamlu's legal system predates the Indian constitution. The deity's main temple in Malana features exquisite stone and wood carvings. Jamlu is considered an extremely strict deity — anyone who breaks village laws or touches sacred objects without permission is fined heavily. The village maintains complete autonomy from state governance in religious matters. Jamlu's annual festival involves elaborate rituals where the deity's decisions on community matters are communicated through the oracle (Gur).

column5: Bijli Mahadev is one of the most dramatic and awe-inspiring Shiva temples in the Himalayas, perched at an altitude of 2,460 meters on the Mathan mountain overlooking the Kullu and Parvati valleys. The temple is famous for its 60-foot-tall sacred staff (flagstaff) that is said to attract divine lightning. When lightning strikes the staff, it shatters the Shiva Lingam inside the temple into pieces. The temple priest then reassembles the Lingam using a special mixture of butter and sattoo (roasted barley flour), and the process of divine destruction and recreation begins anew. This phenomenon is interpreted as Lord Shiva absorbing the evil energies of the universe into himself to protect the world. The panoramic 360-degree views from the temple summit encompass the snow-capped Pir Panjal range, the Beas River valley, and the Parvati Valley. Pilgrims undertake a steep 3-kilometer trek from the road to reach the temple. The site is considered so powerful that even during clear skies, sudden lightning can strike the staff.

column5: Hadimba Devi, also known as Dhungri Mata, is the powerful forest goddess of Manali and the ancestral patron deity of the Kullu royal family. Her magnificent four-tiered wooden pagoda temple was built in 1553 CE by Raja Bahadur Singh in the midst of ancient Deodar cedar forests. The temple is an architectural masterpiece featuring intricate wood carvings of animals, dancers, and celestial beings. Hadimba is identified with the Rakshasi princess from the Mahabharata who married Bhima during the Pandavas' exile. According to local tradition, she chose to remain in the forests of Manali as a benevolent protector rather than accompany the Pandavas. The temple has no idol inside — instead, a large rock formation represents the goddess. During her annual fair in May, the goddess is taken in procession through Manali. Animal sacrifice was historically part of her worship, reflecting her pre-Aryan origins. She is considered the grandmother (Nani) of all Kullu deities. The Kullu kings would seek her blessing before any major military campaign or administrative decision.

column5: Lord Raghunath Ji is the supreme presiding deity of the Kullu Valley, installed in 1651 CE by Raja Jagat Singh after he was guilt-ridden for causing the death of a Brahmin family. The king sent emissaries to Ayodhya who brought back the sacred idol of Lord Rama (Raghunath). Upon installation, the Raja symbolically surrendered his kingdom to the deity, declaring himself merely a regent ruling on behalf of Lord Raghunath. Since then, every administrative order in Kullu was issued in the name of Raghunath Ji. The deity resides in the Raghunath Temple in Sultanpur, the former capital. During the world-famous Kullu Dussehra, over 200 village deities from across the valley are brought in procession to pay homage to Lord Raghunath at Dhalpur Maidan. This seven-day festival, declared of International importance by the Government of India, begins on Vijaya Dashami when other Dussehra celebrations end. The grand Rath Yatra (chariot procession) of Raghunath Ji through the town is the centerpiece event. The deity's treasury contains centuries of gold, silver and precious jewels offered by devotees and rulers.
